title: Spin explained: topspin, backspin and sidespin
seo_title: Table tennis spin explained: topspin, backspin, sidespin
description: How spin works in table tennis: what topspin, backspin and sidespin do, how to make each one, how to read it and how to angle your bat to return it.
summary: Spin is what makes table tennis hard to play and fascinating to watch. Here is how topspin, backspin and sidespin are made, what they do and how to deal with them.
key_points: You make spin by brushing the ball rather than hitting it flat: the finer the contact, the more spin.
Topspin makes the ball dip; backspin holds it up; sidespin curves it left or right.
Spin also changes how the ball comes off your bat: backspin drops into the net, topspin flies long.
Read spin from your opponent's bat at the moment of contact, then adjust your bat angle.
Smooth inverted rubber makes the most spin; pimples and anti-spin rubbers change or reduce it.
body: Spin is the rotation of the ball, and in table tennis it shapes almost every point. There are three kinds. Topspin, where the top of the ball rotates forwards, makes it dip on to the table. Backspin, where the bottom rotates forwards, holds the ball up and makes it hard to attack. Sidespin makes it curve and kick sideways. You create spin by brushing the ball with the rubber, and you return it by angling your bat to cancel out what is on the ball.
## How spin is made

Hit the ball flat and it goes back with little spin. Brush it, so the rubber moves across the ball as well as through it, and it spins. USA Table Tennis's instructors' guide puts it simply: "The more you graze the ball, the more spin you get." A stroke that brushes upwards gives topspin, downwards gives backspin and sideways gives sidespin. Most shots mix them: a serve can carry backspin and sidespin at once.

The rubber matters. Butterfly says smooth inverted rubber, with the pimples facing inwards, has "a large contact area for the ball, which makes it easy to impart spin", and tacky rubbers grip the ball even more. Our guide to [rubbers](/guide/table-tennis-rubbers-explained.html) explains the types.

A spinning ball drags air round with it, so the pressure on one side becomes lower than on the other, and the ball curves towards the low-pressure side. This is the Magnus effect, and the force always acts at right angles to the ball's direction of travel. Researchers presenting to the American Physical Society in 2012 noted that "the smaller and lighter table tennis ball is at the mercy of the Magnus effect", which is why spin bends its path so much more than in most ball games.
## Topspin

With topspin the Magnus force pushes the ball down, so it can be hit hard and still dip on to the table. That makes topspin the basis of attacking play: USATT's guide notes that "topspin is used on nearly all attacking shots". The loop, a long brushing stroke from below the ball, is the heaviest topspin shot.

When topspin hits your bat it tends to fly upwards and long. To return it, close the bat (tilt the face forwards, towards the table) and, in USATT's words, "aim down or the ball will pop up or go off the end". The easiest answer is often to play topspin back, as Table Tennis England's notes for new league players advise.
## Backspin

Backspin works the other way. The ball tends to float, travelling flatter and holding up in the air, and it is the spin of control and defence: pushes, the short backspin strokes played over the table, and chops, the long defensive strokes of [choppers](/guide/table-tennis-playing-styles.html).

Backspin dives downwards off your bat, so the classic beginner's mistake is to push or block it straight into the net. Open the bat (tilt the face back, towards the ceiling) and lift. USATT says "you have to aim up to compensate for the spin". Against short backspin you can push it back, or, as you improve, attack it with a flick, a short wristy topspin stroke.
## Sidespin

Sidespin makes the ball curve in the air and kick sideways off the table and your bat. It is most common on serves, often combined with topspin or backspin. Table Tennis England's advice is to "hit towards where the bat has come from": if the server's bat moved from your left to your right, aim to your left to cancel the kick.
## Reading spin

The ball itself is usually spinning too fast to read, so watch your opponent's bat at the moment of contact: its direction, its speed and its angle. Good servers try to hide that. Table Tennis Scotland's coaching cards say "the contact is the key factor for disguise" and the aim is to make "different spins look as similar as possible". That includes the float, a serve with little or no spin dressed up to look like one that has plenty.

The laws help you a little. The server must toss the ball "without imparting spin", so all the spin comes from the bat, and must not hide the ball from you. The two sides of every bat must be different colours, black and a bright colour, so you can see which rubber was used. Our guide to [legal serves](/guide/legal-serve-rules.html) has the full rules.
## Rubbers, balls and spin

Not every bat sends your spin back the same way. Pimples-out rubber is less affected by the spin on the ball. Long pimples, says USATT, "return any spin given to them", so your heavy topspin can come back as backspin. Anti-spin rubber has almost no grip. Table Tennis England's advice against anti-spin is not to load the ball with spin, because it gives you back your own spin.

Changes to the ball have reduced spin at the top level. When the 40mm ball replaced the 38mm one in 2000, the ITTF cited tests showing it was 3% to 6% less spinny, and Timo Boll has said the move to plastic balls from 2014 "cut down the rotation". Our [guide to balls](/guide/table-tennis-balls-explained.html) tells the story.
## Your next step

Practise against spin before trying to make lots of it. Ask a club partner to serve you backspin and topspin until you can adjust your bat angle without thinking. Then turn to the serve, where spin does most damage: our guide to [serve and receive tactics](/guide/serve-and-receive-tactics.html) explains why.
